question: A customer raises three separate issues during one session: a refund inquiry (turns 1-15), a subscription question (turns 16-30), and a payment method update (turns 31-45). At turn 48, the customer asks "What happened with my refund?" The conversation is approaching context limits. What strategy best maintains the agent's ability to address all issues throughout the session?
optionA: Extract and persist structured issue data (order IDs, amounts, statuses) into a separate context layer.
optionB: Summarize earlier turns into a narrative description, preserving full message history only for the active issue.
optionC: Rely on MCP tools to re-fetch relevant information on demand when the customer references earlier issues.
optionD: Implement sliding window context that retains the most recent 30 turns.
explanation:
Extracting and persisting structured issue data - order IDs, amounts, statuses - into a separate context layer is structured note-taking, one of the three techniques Anthropic's context-engineering guidance names for holding an agent together past the context window (the other two are compaction and multi-agent architectures). It is the only one of the four options under which a specific identifier from turn 3 survives verbatim to turn 48, which is what "What happened with my refund?" needs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (summarise earlier turns into a narrative, keep full history only for the active issue) — this is compaction, a real technique rather than a wrong one, but it is lossy by design: summarising "can result in the loss of subtle but critical context whose importance only becomes apparent later", which is exactly the refund detail the customer is about to ask for.
Option C (rely on MCP tools to re-fetch on demand) — only works while the agent still knows which order to fetch, and that identifier is the thing option A exists to keep.
Option D (sliding window of the most recent 30 turns) — discards the refund and subscription issues outright; at turn 48 the window has already dropped everything before turn 19.
References:
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

question: A developer wants Claude to consistently answer as an experienced cybersecurity analyst regardless of the user question. Which prompt component should contain this instruction?
optionA: User message
optionB: Assistant response
optionC: System prompt
optionD: Retrieved document
explanation:
The system prompt is where a persistent role instruction belongs. It establishes behavioural instructions that apply throughout the conversation - role definition, response style, organisational policies - and Claude prioritises system instructions above ordinary user requests whenever possible, which is what "regardless of the user question" requires.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (user message) — scoped to a single turn, so the persona would have to be restated on every question and a later user message could simply override it.
Option B (assistant response) — Claude's output rather than an instruction channel; placing the role there prefills one reply instead of governing the whole conversation.
Option D (retrieved document) — reference content for Claude to read, not a directive about how to answer; documents carry facts, not behavioural authority.
References:
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

question:
You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
When researching "renewable energy adoption," the web search agent returns recent statistics (2024: 35% adoption) while the document analysis agent extracts data from internal reports (2021: 18% adoption). The synthesis agent incorrectly flags these as contradictory sources rather than recognizing the data shows growth over time. What change would best enable the synthesis agent to correctly interpret such temporal differences?
optionA: Instruct the synthesis agent to always treat the most recent data as authoritative and place older findings in a separate historical appendix.
optionB: Add a conflict resolution agent that automatically discards older data when newer data exists for the same metric.
optionC: Require subagents to include publication or data collection dates in their structured outputs.
optionD: Configure the web search agent to only return results from the past 6 months.
explanation:
Requiring subagents to include publication or data-collection dates in their structured outputs lets the synthesis agent read 18% in 2021 and 35% in 2024 as one trend rather than two claims in conflict.
The reason the metadata has to travel inside each subagent's output is that subagent context is not shared. A subagent's context window starts fresh with no parent conversation, and only its final message returns to the coordinator, so anything the search agent knew but did not write down - including when a figure was measured - is unrecoverable downstream.
This is agent-design judgment rather than a documented rule. The reference establishes the context boundary the answer turns on, not the answer itself.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (treat the most recent data as authoritative, older findings in an appendix) — a blanket recency rule assumes any disagreement is an error rather than a time series, so the 2021 figure is demoted instead of read as the starting point of the growth.
Option B (conflict-resolution agent that discards older data) — destroys the information rather than labelling it; the growth the report exists to describe disappears with the older figure.
Option D (web search limited to the past 6 months) — narrows the search window without touching the document-analysis agent, so the 2021 internal figure still arrives undated and the same false conflict is flagged.
References:
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

question: After the web search agent finds 25 sources (120K tokens of raw content), the document analysis agent extracts key insights (15K tokens), and the synthesis agent produces a coherent narrative draft (3K tokens), the coordinator must pass context to the report generation agent for the final output with proper source citations. What context-passing strategy provides the best balance of completeness and efficiency?
optionA: Pass the full accumulated context from all prior agents.
optionB: Pass the synthesis draft along with a structured source index that maps key claims to their source URLs and relevant excerpts.
optionC: Pass only the synthesis draft and have a separate post-processing pipeline match claims to sources and insert citations after the report is generated.
optionD: Pass a condensed summary of all prior stages that preserves the main findings and attributes them to sources by name only.
explanation:
Passing the synthesis draft along with a structured source index that maps key claims to their source URLs and excerpts gives the report generator the two things it needs: the narrative to render, and enough provenance to cite it. That is roughly 3K tokens plus the index rather than the 138K the earlier stages consumed.
This is design judgment rather than a documented rule; the references establish the context-window constraint and the subagent output boundary it works within.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (pass the full accumulated context) — spends context on 120K tokens of raw sources the drafting stage has already distilled, and longer context measurably degrades recall, the effect Anthropic describes as context rot.
Option C (synthesis draft only, citations matched in post-processing) — asks a later pass to re-derive which source supported which sentence, a mapping the synthesis stage already had and threw away.
Option D (condensed summary attributing findings to sources by name only) — leaves the generator unable to produce a checkable citation, since a name without a URL or excerpt cannot be verified.
References:
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

question: A customer writes: "I've been going back and forth on this return for days. I just want to speak to someone who can actually help me." The agent has confirmed via lookup_order that the return is straightforward - within policy and eligible for immediate processing. What should the agent do?
optionA: Process the refund via process_refund to resolve the underlying issue, then inform them it's complete
optionB: Acknowledge frustration, inform them this is resolvable now, and offer to complete it or escalate
optionC: Call escalate_to_human immediately to honor the customer's request
optionD: Ask what specifically hasn't worked in previous attempts before deciding whether to escalate or resolve automatically
explanation:
Acknowledging the frustration, telling the customer that this is resolvable now, and offering to complete it or escalate is the only response which treats both facts in the stem as true at once: the customer wants a person, and lookup_order has already established that the return is within policy and eligible for processing.
This is service-design judgment; no vendor page settles it. The reference is orienting rather than decisive - it establishes only the general pattern of returning to the human at blockers and checkpoints.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (process the refund, then inform them) — delivers the fix but takes an irreversible action on the account without asking, moments after the customer said what they wanted.
Option C (call escalate_to_human immediately) — hands the conversation onward but throws away a fix the agent can finish in a single step, adding a queue to a complaint that is already about delay.
Option D (ask what has not worked before deciding) — opens a diagnosis of earlier failures that the eligibility check has already made unnecessary.
References:
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

question: Your process_refund tool returns two types of errors: technical errors ("503 Service Unavailable", "Connection timeout") that are transient (5% of calls), and business errors ("Order exceeds 30 day return window", "Item already refunded") that are permanent (12% of calls). Monitoring shows the agent wastes 3-4 turns retrying business errors that can never succeed. Currently, both error types return only a plain text message to Claude. What's the most effective way to reduce wasted retries while improving customer-facing response quality?
optionA: Implement automatic retry logic at the tool level for technical errors only, passing business errors to Claude without retries.
optionB: Add few-shot examples showing how to distinguish retriable from non-retriable errors by parsing error message text.
optionC: Return structured error responses with retriable: false for business errors and a customer-friendly explanation for Claude to use.
optionD: Add a check_refund_eligibility tool that must be called before process_refund to prevent business rule violations.
explanation:
Returning structured error responses that mark business errors retriable: false and carry a customer-friendly explanation lets the agent distinguish permanent business-rule failures from transient technical failures without parsing plain text. The non-retriable flag ends the 3-4 wasted turns, and the explanation gives Claude something clear and useful to say to the customer, which is the second half of what the stem asks for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (tool-level retries for technical errors only) — handles the 5% transient case inside the tool but still hands business errors to Claude as plain text, so nothing tells it to stop retrying them or what to tell the customer.
Option B (few-shot examples for parsing error text) — teaches Claude to infer from prose what the tool could state directly; every new error message becomes another case to teach.
Option D (mandatory check_refund_eligibility call first) — adds a call to every refund to pre-empt the 12% case, does nothing for the transient errors, and leaves the response quality on a failed refund exactly where it was.
References:
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

question:
You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.
An engineer asks your agent to identify untested code paths in a legacy payment processing module spanning 45 files. After reading the first 8 source files, the agent's responses are becoming noticeably less accurate. It's forgetting previously discussed code patterns and hasn't yet located all test files or traced critical payment flows. What's the most effective approach to complete this investigation?
optionA: Switch to using Grep to search for specific function names instead of reading full files, reducing the content loaded into context for remaining exploration.
optionB: Spawn subagents to investigate specific questions (e.g., "find all test files for payment processing," "trace refund flow dependencies") while the main agent coordinates findings and preserves high-level understanding.
optionC: Document all current findings in a summary report, clear context completely, then use that report as the sole reference for continuing the investigation.
optionD: Clear context with /clear, then selectively re-read only the most critical files discovered so far, writing key findings to a scratchpad file that persists between context resets.
explanation:
Spawning subagents to investigate specific questions - finding the test files, tracing the refund flow - while the main agent coordinates isolates the detailed exploration in separate context windows. Each subagent returns concise findings, so the main agent's context stops degrading while it keeps the high-level understanding across test discovery and payment-flow tracing.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Grep for function names instead of reading files) — slows the growth of context but does not recover the accuracy already lost, and a search for names cannot trace a payment flow across 45 files.
Option C (summary report, clear context, continue from the report alone) — throws away everything the summary omitted and leaves a single context to fill up again on the remaining 37 files.
Option D (/clear, re-read the critical files, keep a scratchpad) — pays the same reset cost and then puts the same files back into the one window that was already overflowing.
References:
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

question: Your content curation agent discovers articles, analyzes each for relevance, then adds selected articles to themed collections. With separate discover_articles(topic), analyze_article(id), and add_to_collection(article_id, collection_id) tools, you observe 18+ sequential tool calls per request, causing latency issues. The agent must make editorial judgments about which articles fit a collection's theme. This requires seeing all candidates with their analysis scores simultaneously to select a cohesive set. What tool composition best addresses efficiency while preserving editorial judgment?
optionA: Keep all tools separate but implement response caching for analyze_article calls.
optionB: Create a curate_collection(topic, collection_id) tool that handles discovery, analysis, and selection internally using configurable quality thresholds.
optionC: Create a discover_and_analyze(topic) composite tool that returns all candidates with their analysis scores, keeping add_to_collection separate for selective calls.
optionD: Add a preview_curation(topic, collection_id) tool that shows what would be added based on predefined rules, with an approve_curation() tool to confirm.
explanation:
A discover_and_analyze(topic) composite tool that returns all candidates with their analysis scores, with add_to_collection kept separate, collapses the discovery and analysis calls into one while leaving the selection to the agent. Seeing every candidate and its score at once is what the editorial judgment in the stem requires, and the separate add_to_collection call keeps that selection under the agent's control while the sequential call count and latency fall.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (keep all tools separate, cache analyze_article) — a cache saves nothing on first requests, and the 18+ sequential calls remain.
Option B (curate_collection handling discovery, analysis and selection by thresholds) — collapses the workflow into one call but hands the editorial judgment to a numeric threshold, which the stem says must stay with the agent.
Option D (preview_curation plus approve_curation) — the selection is still made by predefined rules and merely shown for approval, so the agent never exercises judgment and two calls are added to do it.
References:
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents

question:
You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
Your automated review jobs take 18 seconds to initialize before Claude begins analyzing code. Profiling reveals that the delay results from automatically discovering hooks, MCP servers, plugins, skills, and multiple nested CLAUDE.md files throughout the monorepo.
You need to reduce startup time while ensuring reviews still enforce the coding standards documented in the root-level CLAUDE.md file.
What is the most effective approach?
optionA: Replace the default prompt using --system-prompt-file ./CLAUDE.md, which bypasses default prompt assembly and loads only the project rules.
optionB: Run in --bare mode and pass --append-system-prompt-file ./CLAUDE.md to load the required project standards explicitly while skipping automatic discovery.
optionC: Run in --bare mode and repeat all review criteria directly in the -p prompt for every invocation.
optionD: Keep the default initialization and add --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections to improve prompt-cache reuse across CI runners.
explanation:
Running in --bare mode and passing --append-system-prompt-file ./CLAUDE.md removes the identified startup work while deliberately restoring the one source of project context the reviews require. Anthropic documents that --bare skips automatic discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md files. It is specifically intended for CI and scripted execution where fast, reproducible startup behavior is more important than loading every locally configured extension.
Because bare mode also skips the root CLAUDE.md, the pipeline must supply that content explicitly. --append-system-prompt-file ./CLAUDE.md loads the standards while retaining Claude Code's default coding-agent behavior and tool guidance.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (--system-prompt-file ./CLAUDE.md to replace the default prompt) — replaces Claude Code's default system prompt wholesale, dropping the coding-agent behaviour and tool guidance the reviews rely on, and is a different lever from the discovery that profiling identified.
Option C (--bare and repeat the criteria in the -p prompt every run) — skips discovery but re-types the standards into every invocation, so the pipeline and the root CLAUDE.md drift apart as the file changes.
Option D (default initialisation plus --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections) — targets prompt-cache reuse, not startup; the discovery of hooks, MCP servers, plugins, skills and nested CLAUDE.md files still runs on every job.
References:
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference

question: A prompt asks Claude to produce Markdown tables. Which addition MOST increases consistency?
optionA: Specify exact column names.
optionB: Increase randomness.
optionC: Remove formatting instructions.
optionD: Omit examples.
explanation:
Specifying exact column names is the addition that most increases consistency. Explicit structural requirements reduce ambiguity: providing exact column names, ordering, and formatting expectations helps Claude consistently generate Markdown tables that downstream users or systems can reliably consume.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (increase randomness) — a higher temperature makes two runs of the same prompt differ more, the opposite of consistency.
Option C (remove formatting instructions) — leaves the table shape to Claude's discretion on every run.
Option D (omit examples) — removes a demonstration of the target format; examples are one of the most reliable ways to pin down structure.
References:
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/increase-consistency
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

question: After deploying automated code review, developers report that approximately 35% of flagged findings are false positives falling into consistent patterns: style suggestions contradicting team conventions, security warnings for patterns that are safe in your deployment context, and performance suggestions that would degrade your specific use case. You want to reduce false positives while maintaining the ability to catch genuine issues. Which approach best enables the model to generalize its judgment to novel code patterns it has not seen before?
optionA: Implement post-processing that uses keyword matching to filter out findings containing terms such as "convention," "context-dependent," or "trade-off."
optionB: Include few-shot examples in your prompt showing annotated code snippets that distinguish acceptable patterns from genuine issues in each category.
optionC: Create a comprehensive written specification of all patterns that should not be flagged, and then include the full documentation in the system prompt.
optionD: Add instructions to your system prompt to "be conservative," "only flag definite issues," and "consider that some patterns may be intentional."
explanation:
Few-shot examples of annotated code snippets that distinguish acceptable patterns from genuine issues teach Claude the actual decision boundaries behind the team's judgments. Contrasting examples can demonstrate why one apparent security pattern is acceptable within the organization's deployment controls while a superficially similar implementation is genuinely unsafe. The same technique can distinguish established style conventions from deviations and intentional performance trade-offs from accidental inefficiencies.
Anthropic identifies relevant, diverse, and clearly structured examples as one of the most reliable ways to improve Claude's accuracy and consistency. Its official prompting guidance recommends examples that closely mirror the production task while covering important variations and edge cases. This encourages generalization based on demonstrated criteria instead of memorization of prohibited wording.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (keyword post-filter on "convention", "context-dependent", "trade-off") — suppresses findings by wording, so a genuine issue that mentions a trade-off is silenced and a false positive that does not is passed; it cannot generalise to code it has not seen.
Option C (comprehensive written specification of every pattern not to flag) — an enumeration; a novel pattern is by definition not on the list, and a long exclusion document consumes context without teaching the criteria behind it.
Option D ("be conservative", "only flag definite issues") — vague directives shift the threshold everywhere, dropping genuine findings alongside the false positives, and give no criterion for a pattern the model has not met.
References:
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

question:
You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
Production monitoring shows that the research phase takes longer than expected. Analysis reveals that the coordinator invokes the web-search subagent, waits for its response, and then invokes the document-analysis subagent. These tasks are independent; neither requires the other's output.
How should you modify the system to run these subagents concurrently?
optionA: Switch both subagents to a Haiku-tier model instead of Sonnet to reduce their individual execution times.
optionB: Structure the coordinator to emit both Agent tool calls - formerly Task tool calls - in a single response rather than across separate conversation turns.
optionC: Add instructions explaining the performance benefits of parallel execution and requesting that the coordinator invoke both subagents simultaneously.
optionD: Create an asynchronous orchestration layer that starts separate coordinator-subagent pairs in parallel and aggregates their results.
explanation:
Structuring the coordinator to emit both Agent tool calls in a single response is what runs the two subagents concurrently: independent subagents run at the same time only if the coordinator asks for them at the same time. Anthropic's SDK documentation gives parallelisation as a primary reason to use subagents at all: multiple subagents can run concurrently, so independent subtasks finish in the time of the slowest one rather than the sum of all of them. Claude invokes them through the Agent tool (formerly the Task tool), and one assistant response can carry more than one tool_use block - so emitting both delegations in a single turn is what produces a parallel group, and issuing them in consecutive turns is exactly what serialises them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (switch both subagents to a Haiku-tier model) — makes each subagent individually faster without removing the serialisation, so the total is still one wait after another.
Option C (instructions explaining the benefits of parallel execution) — asks for the behaviour in prose rather than structuring the turn to produce it.
Option D (asynchronous orchestration layer with parallel coordinator-subagent pairs) — builds an orchestration layer around a capability the SDK already has.
References:
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

question:
You are building developer-productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools - Read, Write, Bash, Grep, and Glob - and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.
Engineers frequently ask the agent to cross-reference code changes with Jira tickets during reviews - checking ticket descriptions, acceptance criteria, and recent comments. This currently requires manually copying and pasting content into conversations. The team wants the agent to access this standard Jira ticket data directly.
What is the most effective approach?
optionA: Use the Bash tool with curl to call Jira's REST API, including authentication headers and parsing JSON responses inline.
optionB: Build a custom MCP server wrapping Jira's API with tools designed specifically for this team's code-review workflow.
optionC: Export Jira tickets to Markdown files in the repository that the agent accesses using the Read tool.
optionD: Integrate an existing Jira MCP server that exposes tickets, comments, and metadata through discoverable tool interfaces.
explanation:
Integrating an existing Jira MCP server that exposes tickets, comments, and metadata through discoverable tool interfaces uses the established integration mechanism without creating unnecessary infrastructure. Anthropic's Claude Code MCP documentation specifically recommends connecting an MCP server when users repeatedly copy information from an external system, such as an issue tracker, into conversations.
Once connected, the server exposes Jira operations through named, schema-defined tools that Claude can discover and invoke directly. This allows the agent to retrieve ticket descriptions, acceptance criteria, comments, and metadata while preserving the server's authentication and access controls.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Bash with curl against Jira's REST API) — puts authentication headers and JSON parsing into ad hoc shell commands on every request, with no schema for Claude to discover and credentials exposed in the command line.
Option B (build a custom MCP server wrapping Jira's API) — the right mechanism but an unnecessary build: the stem asks for standard ticket data, which is exactly what an existing Jira server already exposes.
Option C (export tickets to Markdown files read with the Read tool) — a stale snapshot; descriptions, acceptance criteria and recent comments change between exports, and someone still has to run them.
References:
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp

question: Your MCP server implements a check_availability tool that queries an external calendar API. During testing, you encounter three error conditions: (1) the tool is called with a malformed request missing the required user_email parameter, (2) the calendar API returns a 404 because the specified user doesn't exist in the calendar system, and (3) the calendar API returns a 503 because the service is temporarily unavailable. How should each error be reported according to MCP's error handling design?
optionA: Report all three as tool results with isError: true.
optionB: Report errors 1 and 2 as JSON-RPC protocol errors; report error 3 as a tool result with isError: true.
optionC: Report error 1 as a JSON-RPC protocol error; report errors 2 and 3 as tool results with isError: true.
optionD: Report all three as JSON-RPC protocol errors.
explanation:
Reporting error 1 as a JSON-RPC protocol error and errors 2 and 3 as tool results with isError: true is the split the MCP specification draws. Errors caused by malformed requests (missing required parameters) violate the RPC protocol and should be reported as JSON-RPC errors. Errors returned by the external service (user not found, temporary unavailability) are valid tool execution results and should be reported as tool outputs with isError set to true, allowing the agent to handle them gracefully.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (all three as tool results with isError: true) — treats a call missing its required user_email as a valid execution; the specification reserves protocol errors for unknown tools, invalid arguments and server errors.
Option B (errors 1 and 2 as protocol errors, error 3 as isError) — a user who does not exist in the calendar is the outcome of a well-formed call, not a violation of the protocol, so error 2 belongs in the tool result.
Option D (all three as JSON-RPC protocol errors) — hides the API failures from the model as if the request itself had been malformed, so the agent cannot reason about or recover from them.
References:
https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools

question: Which practice MOST improves prompt maintainability?
optionA: One paragraph containing all instructions.
optionB: Clearly separated sections with headings.
optionC: Random ordering.
optionD: Minimal punctuation.
explanation:
Clearly separated sections with headings are what make a prompt maintainable. A prompt that mixes instructions, context, examples and variable input in one undifferentiated block forces both Claude and the next maintainer to infer where each part begins. Anthropic's guidance is to delimit them explicitly: XML tags "help Claude parse complex prompts unambiguously", and wrapping each type of content in its own tag - <instructions>, <context>, <input> - "reduces misinterpretation".
The same separation is what makes a prompt maintainable, because a later edit can be aimed at one labelled section instead of rewritten through a paragraph.
Note that the documented mechanism is delimiting content types, whether by XML tags or by headings; the vendor guidance is about the separation, not about the markup used to achieve it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (one paragraph containing all instructions) — removes the boundaries, so every edit has to be read against the whole block.
Option C (random ordering) — removes the structure; a maintainer cannot predict where a rule lives, and Claude loses the cues that group related instructions.
Option D (minimal punctuation) — removes the cues that survive inside a section, making even a well-sectioned prompt harder to parse.
References:
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

question: Your post_content tool requires user confirmation before publishing. The current workflow displays "Ready to post to social media. Confirm?" and analytics show users approve 98% of requests within 2 seconds. Post-mortems reveal incidents where posts went to wrong accounts, were scheduled for wrong times, or contained errors - all confirmed by users without catching the mistakes. How should you redesign the confirmation workflow?
optionA: Auto-approve routine posts and only require explicit confirmation for unusual patterns like posting to new accounts or large audiences
optionB: Require users to type a confirmation phrase instead of clicking a button
optionC: Add a mandatory waiting period before the confirm option becomes available
optionD: Include the complete post text, target account, scheduled time, and platform in the confirmation request
explanation:
Including the complete post text, target account, scheduled time and platform in the confirmation request is what turns the step into a control, because a confirmation is only a control if it shows the thing being approved. The MCP specification puts this on the client: clients SHOULD "prompt for user confirmation on sensitive operations" and "show tool inputs to the user before calling the server, to avoid malicious or accidental data exfiltration". A prompt reading "Ready to post to social media. Confirm?" shows none of the inputs, which is why a 98% approval rate in two seconds coexists with posts going to the wrong account.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (auto-approve routine posts, confirm only unusual patterns) — removes the check from the majority of cases while leaving it uninformative in the rest; a wrong account or time on a routine post is exactly the incident in the post-mortems.
Option B (type a confirmation phrase instead of clicking) — adjusts the friction rather than the information; a user cannot catch a wrong scheduled time they were never shown.
Option C (mandatory waiting period before confirm is available) — makes approving slower without making the mistake visible, for the same reason.
References:
https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools

question:
You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
After expanding the agent's MCP tools with delivery-specific capabilities (check_delivery_status, contact_driver, issue_credit, apply_promo_code, update_delivery_address, reschedule_delivery), the total tool count has grown from 4 to 10. Your evaluation suite shows tool selection accuracy has dropped from 88% to 71%. Log analysis reveals the majority of errors involve the agent selecting between semantically overlapping tools - calling issue_credit when process_refund was correct, and calling check_delivery_status when lookup_order already returns the needed data. Which approach structurally eliminates the semantic overlap identified in the logs as the error source?
optionA: Enable the tool search tool with defer_loading on the six new tools, keeping the original four always loaded, so the agent dynamically discovers specialized tools only when needed.
optionB: Split the tools across two sub-agents - a "financial resolution" agent with process_refund, issue_credit and apply_promo_code, and a "delivery operations" agent with the remaining delivery tools - with a coordinator routing between them.
optionC: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt demonstrating correct selection for each ambiguous tool pair, such as showing when issue_credit applies versus when process_refund is appropriate.
optionD: Consolidate semantically overlapping tools - merge issue_credit and process_refund into a single resolve_compensation tool with an action parameter, and fold check_delivery_status into lookup_order with an optional include_tracking flag.
explanation:
Consolidating the semantically overlapping tools - merging issue_credit and process_refund into one resolve_compensation tool with an action parameter, and folding check_delivery_status into lookup_order behind an include_tracking flag - removes the competing definitions themselves. Anthropic's guidance is the same move: consolidate related operations into fewer tools rather than one tool per action, because "fewer, more capable tools reduce selection ambiguity", and overlapping tools "distract agents from pursuing efficient strategies".
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (tool search tool with defer_loading on the six new tools) — the wrong instrument for this scale, and the documentation gives the number: tool selection accuracy degrades once you exceed 30 to 50 available tools, which is what the tool search tool and defer_loading exist to fix. This agent has ten. Deferring six of them would hide the overlap rather than remove it - the two tools still compete whenever search surfaces both.
Option B (split across a financial agent and a delivery agent with a coordinator) — moves the ambiguity into a routing decision between agents; issue_credit and process_refund both still exist, and the coordinator now has to make the same semantic call the agent was getting wrong.
Option C (few-shot examples for each ambiguous tool pair) — teaches the boundary case by case without changing the surface that produced it, so the next overlapping pair starts the problem again.
References:
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents

question: Your track_shipment(tracking_id) tool queries an external logistics API that sometimes fails - the API may be temporarily unavailable, the tracking ID may be malformed, or the shipment may not exist. Currently, your tool raises a Python exception when errors occur. Users report the agent gives unhelpful responses like "I'm having trouble with that request" instead of suggesting alternatives, such as verifying the tracking number format or checking by order number. How should you handle errors in tool results?
optionA: Return a generic error response (e.g., {"success": false, "error": "lookup_failed"}) for all failure cases to maintain a consistent schema and avoid exposing internal error details.
optionB: Return structured error information as normal tool output including error type, recoverability status, and actionable context for the user.
optionC: Create dedicated error-recovery tools (retry_tracking_lookup, search_by_order_number) that the model can invoke after the primary tracking tool returns a failure indicator.
optionD: Implement retry logic with exponential backoff inside the tool implementation so transient errors are automatically handled and only return a result after all retry attempts are exhausted.
explanation:
Returning structured error information as normal tool output - error type, recoverability status, and actionable context for the user - is the shape Anthropic's tool-use documentation prescribes for a failed tool result: return the error in the tool result content with is_error set to true, and "write instructive error messages. Instead of generic errors like 'failed', include what went wrong and what Claude should try next (for example, 'Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds.'). This gives Claude the context it needs to recover or adapt without guessing."
That maps directly onto the three failures in the stem: a malformed tracking ID, a shipment that does not exist, and a temporarily unavailable API each want a different next step from the agent, and only a structured result distinguishes them. Raising an exception, which is what the tool does today, returns nothing for Claude to reason about.
One note on provenance: the exam dump this question came from prints its answer as A while supplying the explanation for B. The documentation settles it as B.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (generic {"success": false, "error": "lookup_failed"} for every failure) — the generic response the documentation warns against, and what produces "I'm having trouble with that request": the agent cannot tell a malformed ID from an outage.
Option C (dedicated retry_tracking_lookup and search_by_order_number recovery tools) — adds tools to recover information the first result could have carried.
Option D (exponential backoff inside the tool, returning only after retries are exhausted) — delays every permanent failure, such as a malformed ID, by the full backoff before the agent learns anything, and still says nothing about what went wrong.
References:
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

question:
You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.
Your team frequently migrates React components to Vue. You've written a step-by-step workflow for Claude Code to follow during each migration, and you want every developer on the team to invoke it by typing /migrate-component. The workflow should stay in sync as the team iterates on it. Where should you place the skill file?
optionA: In ~/.claude/skills/migrate-component/SKILL.md on each developer's machine
optionB: In .claude/skills/migrate-component/SKILL.md at the project root, committed to version control
optionC: In the project's .claude/settings.json using a skillOverrides entry to register and define the workflow
optionD: As a detailed instruction block in the project's root CLAUDE.md file
explanation:
A SKILL.md at .claude/skills/migrate-component/ in the project root, committed to version control, is a project-scoped skill: it is available to everyone working in that repository and stays synchronized through version control as the team iterates. The skill directory name exposes it as /migrate-component.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (~/.claude/skills on each developer's machine) — personal scope; every developer holds a private copy that drifts as the workflow changes, which is the opposite of staying in sync.
Option C (a skillOverrides entry in .claude/settings.json) — settings.json holds configuration such as permissions and hooks; a skill is defined by its SKILL.md directory, and no settings entry registers or defines a workflow.
Option D (an instruction block in the root CLAUDE.md) — loads into every session whether or not a migration is happening, and provides no /migrate-component command to invoke.
References:
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills

question: You're implementing the escalation logic for when the agent should call escalate_to_human. Your team proposes four different approaches for triggering escalation. Which approach will most reliably identify cases that genuinely require human intervention?
optionA: Implement sentiment analysis that monitors for frustration indicators (negative language, repeated questions, exclamation marks) and trigger escalation when the frustration score exceeds a configured threshold.
optionB: Configure the agent to escalate after three consecutive tool calls that fail to resolve the customer's stated issue, ensuring a reasonable attempt before involving a human.
optionC: Instruct the agent to escalate when the customer requests a human, when the issue requires policy exceptions, or when the agent cannot make meaningful progress.
optionD: Build a rules engine that maps specific issue types, customer segments, and product categories to escalation decisions, removing the need for model judgment calls.
explanation:
Instructing the agent to escalate when the customer requests a human, when the issue requires a policy exception, or when it cannot make meaningful progress names three triggers that between them cover the distinct reasons a human is actually needed: the customer asked for one, the resolution would exceed the agent's authority, or the agent has stopped making progress. Anthropic's agent guidance describes the same last case structurally - agents pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when encountering blockers.
This is escalation-policy design rather than a documented rule; the reference is orienting rather than decisive.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (sentiment analysis with a frustration threshold) — fires on tone, so it escalates a cheerfully worded policy exception late and a brusque but resolvable question early.
Option B (escalate after three consecutive failed tool calls) — measures effort rather than progress; three failed calls against a genuinely transient backend is not the same event as three against a request the agent cannot fulfil.
Option D (rules engine mapping issue types and segments to escalation) — handles the categories anticipated when it was written and has nothing to say about the ones that were not, which is the population that most needs a human.
References:
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

question: An architect needs Claude to produce structured JSON that downstream software can parse automatically. Which prompting strategy is BEST?
optionA: Ask Claude to "respond normally."
optionB: Use multiple unrelated examples.
optionC: Explicitly specify the required JSON schema and formatting rules.
optionD: Increase maximum output tokens only.
explanation:
Explicitly specifying the required JSON schema and formatting rules is the strategy, because a downstream parser needs a fixed shape and the way to get one is to state it: name the fields, their types, and the nesting, rather than describing the output in prose. Anthropic's structured outputs feature is built on exactly this input - "create a JSON schema that describes the structure you want Claude to follow" - and constrains generation so responses are schema-compliant and parseable.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (ask Claude to "respond normally") — sets no contract at all, so the shape is left to chance on every call.
Option B (multiple unrelated examples) — demonstrate variety rather than a target structure, so they teach the wrong invariant.
Option D (increase maximum output tokens only) — changes how much output is allowed, not what form it takes; a truncated response is a different failure from a misshapen one.
References:
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

question: An organization wants predictable outputs for automated invoice classification. Which API parameter should generally be LOWER?
optionA: Temperature
optionB: Prompt length
optionC: Max tokens
optionD: Context window
explanation:
Temperature is the parameter to lower, because it is the sampling parameter that controls randomness. Anthropic's glossary defines it directly: "Temperature is a parameter that controls the randomness of a model's predictions during text generation... Lower temperatures result in more conservative and deterministic outputs that stick to the most probable phrasing and answers." For invoice classification, where the same document should always land in the same category, that determinism is the property you want.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (prompt length) — describes how much text goes in; shortening it constrains size while leaving the variability between two runs of the same input untouched.
Option C (max tokens) — caps how much can come out; a shorter classification is not a more predictable one.
Option D (context window) — a model property describing how much the model can read, not a knob that affects randomness.
References:
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/glossary

question: Your order management system requires tools for three distinct operations: issuing refunds (requires amount and reason), canceling orders (requires reason), and requesting reshipments (requires shipping address). Each operation shares an order_id parameter but has different additional requirements. You notice during testing that with your current unified tool design, the agent frequently omits required parameters or includes irrelevant ones. What design change will most effectively improve parameter accuracy?
optionA: Keep one unified tool with a nested operation_details object parameter whose internal structure varies by operation type, documented in the tool description.
optionB: Keep one unified tool but add JSON Schema if-then-else conditionals to enforce that parameters like amount are required only when the operation type is "refund".
optionC: Split into three separate tools (issue_refund, cancel_order, request_reshipment), each defining only the parameters required for that specific operation.
optionD: Keep one unified tool with all parameters marked optional, but add detailed few-shot examples in the system prompt showing correct parameter combinations for each operation type.
explanation:
Splitting into three separate tools - issue_refund, cancel_order, request_reshipment - each declaring only the parameters that operation actually takes means issue_refund requires amount and reason, cancel_order requires reason, and request_reshipment requires a shipping address. Each schema's required array then means something enforceable, which is what the observed failure - omitted required parameters and irrelevant included ones - is asking for. Anthropic's guidance supports giving each tool a clear, distinct purpose, and strict tool use (strict: true) can guarantee the inputs match the schema exactly.
Be careful about generalising from this, because the same vendor guidance pushes the other way on tool count. Anthropic explicitly recommends consolidating related operations into fewer tools - "rather than creating a separate tool for every action (create_pr, review_pr, merge_pr), group them into a single tool with an action parameter" - because fewer, more capable tools reduce selection ambiguity, and selection accuracy degrades as the catalogue grows. Splitting improves parameter accuracy at some cost to selection clarity; it does not improve both. Note also that the documented consolidation pattern, one tool with an action parameter, is not among this item's options, and that this deck's tool-overlap question keys that pattern as correct on a different tool set.
Among the options offered, C remains the best answer for the stated symptom.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (one unified tool with a nested operation_details object that varies by operation) — the varying nested structure is itself a source of the ambiguity; the schema cannot say which inner fields are required for which operation, so the omissions continue.
Option B (one unified tool with JSON Schema if-then-else conditionals) — not the documented mechanism for schema conformance, and the agent still sees a single tool advertising every parameter at once, which is the surface that produced the errors.
Option D (all parameters optional plus few-shot examples of correct combinations) — marks every parameter optional, discarding the requirement it needs to enforce, and asks examples to carry what the schema no longer states.
References:
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents

corrected.note: Answer stands. The explanation claimed separate tools "reduce ambiguity during tool selection", which runs against Anthropic's documented guidance: consolidating related operations behind an action parameter is what reduces selection ambiguity, and selection accuracy falls as tool count rises. Splitting buys parameter accuracy, not selection accuracy. The documented pattern is also absent from the option set.

question: Your agent uses three tools: get_property_details(property_id) returns data including street address, get_price_history(property_id) returns historical pricing, and get_neighborhood_info(address) returns area statistics. You observe that get_neighborhood_info always requires get_property_details first just to extract the address, even when users specify the property by ID. This creates unnecessary latency and failure coupling - if the first call fails, the neighborhood request also fails. What tool design change best addresses this?
optionA: Create a lookup_address(property_id) helper tool for retrieving addresses.
optionB: Add retry logic and timeout handling to get_property_details.
optionC: Change get_neighborhood_info to accept property_id, resolving the address internally.
optionD: Consolidate into a single get_property_with_neighborhood(property_id) tool returning both datasets.
explanation:
Changing get_neighborhood_info to accept property_id and resolve the address internally removes the need for the agent to chain through another tool just to extract an intermediate value. Allowing the neighborhood tool to accept the same identifier the user provides reduces latency, avoids the dependency on a prior tool call, and makes the workflow more reliable.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a lookup_address(property_id) helper tool) — still a two-call chain; it swaps the first call for a smaller one, and the latency and failure coupling stay.
Option B (retry logic and timeouts on get_property_details) — makes the dependency more reliable without removing it, and retries make the latency worse rather than better.
Option D (a single get_property_with_neighborhood tool returning both datasets) — fetches both datasets on every call even when only one is wanted, and removes the ability to ask for neighborhood data alone.
References:
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents

question: Your update_user_profile tool accepts a user_id (required) and an optional fields_to_update object. In testing, Claude frequently omits user_id or passes incorrectly structured data. What is most critical for helping Claude understand what parameter values to provide?
optionA: Strict JSON Schema type constraints marking user_id as required and defining fields_to_update as an object type
optionB: Verbose parameter names encoding format hints, such as user_id_string_uuid_format
optionC: Detailed error responses explaining why invalid parameter values were rejected
optionD: Clear parameter descriptions explaining expected format, such as "user_id: UUID of the user to update (required)"
explanation:
Clear parameter descriptions explaining the expected format, such as "user_id: UUID of the user to update (required)", are what Anthropic's tool-definition guidance ranks first, and it ranks them explicitly over schema constraints: "Provide extremely detailed descriptions. This is by far the most important factor in tool performance." The list of what a description should cover names this case directly - "what each parameter means and how it affects the tool's behavior" - and the guidance repeats the ordering elsewhere: "Prioritize descriptions, but consider using input_examples for complex tools."
The documentation also addresses the exact symptom in the stem. On invalid tool calls, including missing required parameters, it says the failure "usually means that there wasn't enough information for Claude to use the tool correctly", and that "your best bet during development is to try the request again with more-detailed description values in your tool definitions".
Where schema-level enforcement is the goal, the documented mechanism is strict tool use (strict: true), which guarantees inputs match the schema - not ordinary type constraints, and not what option A describes.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (strict JSON Schema type constraints marking user_id required and fields_to_update an object) — not wrong so much as insufficient, and the part already in place: the required array and the object type are standard in every documented tool definition, and this tool has them while still being called incorrectly. A schema states that user_id is required; it does not say what a valid one looks like.
Option B (verbose parameter names such as user_id_string_uuid_format) — encodes format hints in the parameter name, which the guidance puts in the description instead.
Option C (detailed error responses explaining rejected values) — corrects errors after they happen rather than preventing them, so the first call is still wrong.
References:
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

corrected.note: Key moved A to D. Anthropic's tool-use documentation states that detailed descriptions are "by far the most important factor in tool performance", explains that each parameter's meaning belongs there, and prescribes more-detailed descriptions as the fix for exactly this failure - Claude omitting a required parameter. The imported source keyed A while its own explanation argued only that a schema states requirements, which the tool already did.

question: Compliance requires that refunds exceeding $500 must automatically escalate to a human agent - this rule cannot be left to model discretion. Despite clear system prompt instructions, production logs show the agent occasionally processes high-value refunds directly (3% failure rate). How should you achieve guaranteed compliance?
optionA: Modify the refund tool to return an error with message "Amount exceeds policy limit - please escalate" when threshold is exceeded.
optionB: Add few-shot examples to the prompt showing correct escalation behavior at various refund amounts ($400, $500, $600).
optionC: Implement a hook to intercept tool calls; when the refund process amount exceeds $500, block it and invoke human escalation.
optionD: Strengthen the system prompt with emphatic language: "CRITICAL POLICY: Refunds over $500 MUST trigger human escalation. NEVER process these directly."
explanation:
A hook that intercepts tool calls and, when the refund amount exceeds $500, blocks the call and invokes human escalation enforces the policy outside the model. A PreToolUse hook runs before the tool executes and can block it deterministically, so the rule is applied consistently regardless of prompt instructions or agent behavior - which is what "cannot be left to model discretion" requires.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (refund tool returns an "Amount exceeds policy limit - please escalate" error) — stops the refund at the tool, but the escalation is still left to the model to act on after reading the message, so it is not automatic.
Option B (few-shot examples at $400, $500, $600) — prompt-level guidance, subject to the same 3% class of failure the stem reports for instructions that are already clear.
Option D (emphatic "CRITICAL POLICY ... NEVER" language) — still a prompt instruction; the stem states that clear instructions already fail 3% of the time, and louder wording does not turn discretion into enforcement.
References:
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks

question: Production logs reveal inconsistent error handling: when lookup_order fails, the agent sometimes retries 5+ times (wasteful when the order ID doesn't exist), sometimes escalates immediately (premature for temporary network issues), and sometimes asks users for clarification (inappropriate when the issue is a backend permission error). Investigation shows your MCP tool returns uniform error responses: {"isError": true, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Operation failed"}]}. The agent cannot distinguish between error types. What's the most effective improvement?
optionA: Create an analyze_error MCP tool the agent calls after any failure to determine the error category and recommended action.
optionB: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt demonstrating how to interpret error message patterns and select appropriate responses for each.
optionC: Enhance error responses with structured metadata: include errorCategory (transient/validation/permission), isRetryable boolean, and a description of what caused the failure.
optionD: Implement retry logic with exponential backoff in your MCP server for all errors, returning to the agent only after retries are exhausted.
explanation:
Enhancing the error responses with structured metadata - an errorCategory of transient, validation or permission, an isRetryable boolean, and a description of what caused the failure - gives the agent the information it needs to choose the right recovery path. By distinguishing transient, validation, and permission failures, and by explicitly indicating whether retry is appropriate, the agent can avoid wasteful retries, premature escalation, and unnecessary user clarification.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an analyze_error tool called after any failure) — a second call to recover information the first result could have carried, and it can only classify "Operation failed" if the cause was recorded somewhere the agent cannot see.
Option B (few-shot examples for interpreting error message patterns) — there is no pattern to interpret; the message is the identical "Operation failed" for every failure.
Option D (exponential backoff in the MCP server for all errors) — retries the non-existent order ID and the permission error too, delaying every permanent failure and still returning the same undifferentiated result at the end.
References:
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls
https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools

question: When implementing your lookup_order MCP tool, the backend sometimes returns errors (e.g., "Order not found" or temporary database failures). What is the correct pattern for communicating these errors back to the agent?
optionA: Throw an exception from the tool handler so the agent framework can catch and log it
optionB: Return the error message in the tool result content with the isError flag set to true
optionC: Log the error server-side and return an empty result to avoid confusing the model
optionD: Return a success response with a "status" field indicating the error type
explanation:
Returning the error message in the tool result content with the isError flag set to true is the MCP pattern for a failure inside the tool: the agent receives an explicit error signal while the message is preserved. This enables the agent to reason about the failure, choose appropriate recovery actions, and provide meaningful feedback to the user.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (throw an exception from the handler) — surfaces as a protocol-level failure for the framework to log; the model gets no message to reason about and cannot tell "Order not found" from a database outage.
Option C (log server-side and return an empty result) — the model sees an empty success and may report that no order exists or invent a result, since it was never told anything failed.
Option D (a success response with a "status" field) — hides a failure inside a success; the isError flag is the signal the client and model look at, and a status field buried in a success payload is easy to overlook.
References:
https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools
